On 11 ScienceWorld task types (245 episodes), death avoidance accounts for 90.41\\% of routing signal ($\\Delta_{\\text{full}} = +29.60 \\rightarrow \\Delta_{\\text{no\\_death}} = +2.84$; $r = 0.9698$, $p = 8.12 \\times 10^{-7}$). The value of deterministic computation is predominantly concentrated in preventing catastrophic failures (9.6\\% from non-death differences).",
          "+We introduce episode-level counterfactual analysis for understanding routing between LLM internal reasoning and deterministic computation, overcoming per-step oracle degeneracy (98.2\\% tie rate) in sparse-reward settings. On 11 ScienceWorld task types (245 episodes), death avoidance accounts for 90.41\\% of routing signal ($\\Delta_{\\text{full}} = +29.60 \\rightarrow \\Delta_{\\text{no\\_death}} = +2.84$; $r = 0.9698$, $p = 8.12 \\times 10^{-7}$). The value of deterministic computation is predominantly concentrated in preventing catastrophic failures.",
          " ",
          " \\paragraph{Limitations and Future Work.} Our analysis uses a single benchmark (ScienceWorld) with a single LLM backbone (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct). ScienceWorld's $-100$ death penalty may amplify the death avoidance signal; environments with less catastrophic failure modes could exhibit lower DAF values. Our counterfactual labels operate at episode granularity, limiting router training resolution. Cross-seed instability in internal recall (51.5--81.8\\%) warrants further investigation. Step-level labeling with denser rewards (e.g., DAgger-style \\cite{dagger-2011} imitation learning) could improve both decomposition and router training. Extension to code-interpreter routing and multi-LLM evaluation would test generalization beyond simulator-based environments.",
          "\\ No newline at end of file"
        ]
      }

54	\paragraph{Implicit router.} We fine-tune a smaller model (Qwen3-1.7B) to internalize routing decisions within its generation process. Gradient accumulation is critical: with gradient accumulation of 1, the model fails to achieve meaningful routing discrimination (internal recall 26.7\%); with gradient accumulation of 8, the model becomes non-degenerate (internal recall above 50\% across all seeds). We report results for the non-degenerate configuration (gradient accumulation 8). At the logit level, accuracy reaches 65.4\% with balanced accuracy of 59.3\%, demonstrating a weak but above-chance routing signal beyond what a degenerate always-deterministic predictor captures. At the generation level, accuracy and balanced accuracy are identical to the logit level (65.4\% and 59.3\%), though internal recall drops to 51.5\%.
55	
56	\paragraph{Cross-seed stability.} Balanced accuracy is stable across seeds (57--59\%), but internal recall varies from 51.5\% to 81.8\%---the signal exists but is insufficient for practical routing, consistent with the death avoidance decomposition: when ${\sim}90\%$ of routing value is death avoidance, the learnable non-death signal is structurally thin.
```

<details><summary>↩ Tool result · `toolu_01NXfrDest2DL9m4BFfRt2yK`</summary>

```text
1	\begin{abstract}
2	LLM agents in rule-governed interactive environments face catastrophic failures when internal reasoning hallucinates state transitions. Deterministic external computation (environment simulators, code interpreters) can prevent such failures, but what does routing between these modalities actually learn? Per-step oracle labeling degenerates under sparse rewards---on ScienceWorld, 98.2\% of steps produce identical scores regardless of modality. We propose episode-level counterfactual analysis: running complete episodes under pure-internal and pure-deterministic strategies to generate routing labels from episode outcomes. Across 11 ScienceWorld task types (245 episodes), we find that death avoidance accounts for 90.41\% of the routing signal between Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct internal reasoning and deterministic computation ($\Delta_{\text{full}} = +29.60$, $\Delta_{\text{no\_death}} = +2.84$; Pearson $r = 0.9698$, $p = 8.12 \times 10^{-7}$ across task types). When neither strategy causes agent death, performance is near-equivalent. A trained router does not significantly outperform an unconditional always-deterministic strategy ($-10.70$ vs.\ $-9.47$), confirming that the value of deterministic computation in this environment is concentrated in preventing catastrophic failures, not in providing positive task guidance.
3	\end{abstract}
```

The few internally-routed episodes include cases where the agent dies, and misrouting cost exceeds the benefit of correctly routing rare internal-preferred episodes. ```text
1	\section{Experiments}
2	
3	\subsection{Death Avoidance Decomposition}
4	\label{sec:death-decomp}
5	
6	\begin{figure}[t]
7	\centering
8	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig1_daf_scatter.pdf}
9	\caption{Per-task scatter plot: death rate differential (internal minus deterministic) vs.\ performance gap ($\Delta_{\text{full}}$). Pearson $r = 0.9698$ ($p = 8.12 \times 10^{-7}$). Each point is one of 11 ScienceWorld task types.}
10	\label{fig:decomposition}
11	\end{figure}
12	
13	The full performance gap between deterministic and internal strategies across 245 episodes is $\Delta_{\text{full}} = +29.60$ points. When we exclude all episodes where either strategy results in agent death, the gap collapses to $\Delta_{\text{nd}} = +2.84$. The resulting Death Avoidance Factor (\S\ref{sec:daf}) is 90.41\%: approximately 90\% of the deterministic strategy's advantage over internal reasoning is attributable to death avoidance rather than superior task performance when both agents survive.
14	
15	This concentration is consistent across task types (Appendix~\ref{app:per-task}). The Pearson correlation between per-task death rate differential and $\Delta_{\text{full}}$ is $r = 0.9698$ ($p = 8.12 \times 10^{-7}$; bootstrap 95\% CI $[0.952, 0.995]$), as shown in Figure~\ref{fig:decomposition}. Spearman rank correlation is $\rho = 0.986$ ($p = 2.4 \times 10^{-8}$), and leave-one-out analysis shows $r \in [0.963, 0.980]$---no single task type is a leverage point (Appendix~\ref{app:correlation}). We note that death rate differential and $\Delta_{\text{full}}$ are structurally coupled through the penalty term $P$, so high correlation is expected when death dominates. The empirically non-trivial finding is that 78.9\% of non-tie routing labels are driven by death asymmetry independent of $P$. Knowing how much more frequently the internal strategy dies is nearly sufficient to predict the full performance gap for a given task type. The internal strategy dies in 42.9\% of episodes compared to 16.3\% for deterministic computation---a 2.6$\times$ ratio that drives the bulk of the observed score difference.
16	
17	The episode-level label distribution reflects this asymmetry: of 245 episodes, 86 are \texttt{det\_preferred}, only 9 \texttt{internal\_preferred}, and 150 \texttt{no\_preference}---when internal reasoning does not cause death, it performs comparably to deterministic computation.
18	
19	Notably, the per-task DAF distribution is bimodal: \texttt{find-non-living-thing} exhibits DAF $\approx 0\%$ (routing signal entirely from non-death score differences, $\Delta = +9.58$), while all other task types exceed 85\%.
20	
21	One task reveals the residual non-death signal. \texttt{find-non-living-thing} ($n=40$) has zero deaths under both strategies yet shows $\Delta_{\text{full}} = +9.58$, entirely from non-death performance differences---deterministic computation can provide advantages through more accurate state tracking even when agents survive. However, among the 10 death-prone task types, death avoidance overwhelms non-death differences. When both modalities survive, the gap is small but non-negligible ($\Delta_{\text{nd}} = +2.84$, 9.6\% of $\Delta_{\text{full}}$).
22	
23	\subsection{Baselines}
24	\label{sec:baselines}
25	
26	\begin{table}[t]
27	\centering
28	\small
29	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
30	\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
31	\toprule
32	Strategy & Score & 95\% CI & Death \% \\
33	\midrule
34	Always-Internal & $-39.07$ & [$-46.40$, $-32.27$] & 42.9 \\
35	Always-Deterministic & $-9.47$ & [$-14.71$, $-4.29$] & 16.3 \\
36	Random & $-22.38$ & [$-28.67$, $-15.75$] & 27.8 \\
37	Oracle & $-6.58$ & [$-11.54$, $-1.70$] & 14.3 \\
38	\midrule
39	Trained Router$^\dagger$ & $-10.70$ & [$-16.33$, $-5.27$] & 17.6 \\
40	\bottomrule
41	\end{tabular}}
42	\caption{Episode-weighted mean scores on ScienceWorld (11 task types, 245 episodes). 95\% Bootstrap CIs. The oracle selects the higher-scoring strategy per episode; 96.3\% of its decisions match the always-deterministic strategy. $\dagger$\,4-seed mean.}
43	\label{tab:baselines}
44	\end{table}
45	
46	Table~\ref{tab:baselines} reports episode-weighted mean scores and death rates for four unconditional strategies. Always-deterministic ($-9.47$) outperforms always-internal ($-39.07$) by 29.60 points, consistent with $\Delta_{\text{full}}$. The oracle, which selects the higher-scoring strategy per episode, improves only modestly to $-6.58$, with 96.3\% of its routing decisions matching always-deterministic. This \emph{oracle degeneracy} indicates that the optimal episode-level routing policy closely resembles unconditional deterministic computation---the routing signal is insufficient to improve upon simply always choosing the deterministic strategy. Random routing ($-22.38$) falls between the two pure strategies, with a death rate (27.8\%) proportional to its 50/50 allocation.
47	
48	Keyword-based routing fails structurally: match rates cluster at extremes (85.8\% or $<$5\%), precluding meaningful routing discrimination.
49	
50	\subsection{Router Training as Diagnostic}
51	\label{sec:router-diagnostic}
52	
53	A natural question is whether the episode-level counterfactual labels can train a step-level router. We investigate this as a diagnostic probe of label informativeness rather than a routing system proposal, testing two architectures.
54	
55	\paragraph{Classification head.} A linear head on LLM hidden representations, trained on episode-level labels, degenerates to always-deterministic (0\% internal recall) across all configurations (class weighting, focal loss, undersampling, temperature scaling).
56	
57	\paragraph{Implicit router.} We fine-tune Qwen3-1.7B to internalize routing decisions within its generation (Appendix~\ref{app:router-details}). Across four seeds, balanced accuracy is $58.1 \pm 0.8\%$---above chance but insufficient for practical routing, with seed-level variation (Appendix~\ref{app:router-details}) reflecting threshold sensitivity rather than genuine signal.
58	
59	\paragraph{End-to-end evaluation.} Deployed as an episode-level router (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}), the trained router scores $-10.70$ (95\% CI $[-16.33, -5.27]$), not statistically outperforming always-deterministic ($-9.47$, $[-14.71, -4.29]$; overlapping CIs). The episode-to-step granularity mismatch is the bottleneck: when DAF $\approx 90\%$, router headroom is limited to the ${\sim}10\%$ non-death signal.
60	
61	\paragraph{Data split.} Of 245 episodes, 95 non-tie labels are split 85/15 (81 train, 14 validation; 1734/306 steps). Baselines in Table~\ref{tab:baselines} report trajectory statistics; the router score ($-10.70$) comes from fresh environment interaction.
62	
63	\paragraph{Labeling quality.} We verify label quality in Appendix~\ref{app:labeling}.
64	
65	\subsection{Cross-Model Verification}
66	\label{sec:cross-model}
67	
68	To test whether the death avoidance pattern is model-specific, we run a mechanism verification pilot with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on two task types (\texttt{freeze} and \texttt{find-non-living-thing}, 5 episode pairs each, $N{=}10$). Llama-8B achieves lower absolute ScienceWorld scores than Qwen-2.5-7B, reflecting weaker task-level capability, but the death pattern direction is consistent across model families.
69	
70	On \texttt{freeze}, the internal strategy dies in 40\% of episodes versus 20\% for deterministic (Qwen: 55\%/25\%)---the same directional asymmetry. The single non-tie episode arises from death asymmetry: the internal strategy dies while deterministic survives, producing a det-preferred label consistent with the Qwen pattern. On \texttt{find-non-living-thing}, both strategies achieve 0\% death rate under Llama, matching Qwen exactly; the 3 det-preferred labels arise from non-death score differences.
71	
72	\begin{table}[t]
73	\centering
74	\small
75	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
76	\begin{tabular}{@{}llcccc@{}}
77	\toprule
78	Task & Model & D\%\textsubscript{int} & D\%\textsubscript{det} & $\Delta$D\% & D / I / N \\
79	\midrule
80	freeze & Qwen-7B & 55 & 25 & +30 & 6 / 0 / 14 \\
81	freeze & Llama-8B & 40 & 20 & +20 & 1 / 0 / 4 \\
82	\midrule
83	find-non-living & Qwen-7B & 0 & 0 & 0 & 16 / 4 / 20 \\
84	find-non-living & Llama-8B & 0 & 0 & 0 & 3 / 1 / 1 \\
85	\bottomrule
86	\end{tabular}}
87	\caption{Cross-model death rate comparison. Llama pilot: $n{=}5$ episodes per task; Qwen: from Table~\ref{tab:per-task}. $\Delta$D\%: internal minus deterministic death rate. D/I/N: det-preferred / internal-preferred / no-preference labels.}
88	\label{tab:cross-model}
89	\end{table}
90	
91	Table~\ref{tab:cross-model} summarizes the comparison. This pilot ($N{=}10$ episode pairs) provides preliminary directional evidence only: the sample size precludes statistical claims. Nevertheless, observing the same death asymmetry direction in a different model family (Llama vs.\ Qwen) suggests that the pattern reflects a structural property of internal reasoning in interactive environments rather than a model-specific artifact.

Always-deterministic ($-9.47$) outperforms always-internal ($-39.07$) by 29.60 points, consistent with $\\Delta_{\\text{full}}$. The oracle, which selects the higher-scoring strategy per episode, improves only modestly to $-6.58$, with 96.3\\% of its routing decisions matching always-deterministic.         "content": "\\section{Introduction}\n\nLarge language models deployed as interactive agents must repeatedly decide \\emph{how} to compute: reason internally, or delegate to an external tool.\nA Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct agent navigating ScienceWorld \\cite{scienceworld-2022}---a text-based science simulation with 30 task types---faces this choice at every step. Tracking temperature thresholds, container states, and multi-step procedures via internal reasoning is error-prone: the model may hallucinate that water has boiled when the stove was never activated, or that an object has been moved when the action was invalid. Deterministic external computation (environment simulators, code interpreters) eliminates such hallucinations via exact state transitions. The practical question for agent design is therefore: \\emph{when should an agent route computation externally versus reasoning internally?}\n\nExisting routing approaches frame this as a capability or efficiency decision.\nToolformer \\cite{toolformer-2023} teaches models to insert API calls when doing so reduces perplexity; ART \\cite{art-2023} decomposes tasks into tool-augmented programs; Chameleon \\cite{chameleon-2023} selects among heterogeneous modules (search, code, vision) per subtask.\nMore recent adaptive-computation methods route to different reasoning depths \\cite{cogrouter-2026,ares-2026} or model tiers \\cite{mtrouter-2026}.\nThe shared assumption is that routing signal stems from diverse sources---accuracy, latency, capability matching---and that a learned router can exploit this signal to improve over any fixed strategy.\nBut this assumption has never been systematically verified: \\emph{what actually drives the value of routing decisions in interactive environments?}\n\nWe find a surprisingly concentrated answer: \\textbf{death avoidance accounts for approximately 90\\% of the routing signal} in ScienceWorld.\nThe internal strategy's hallucination-induced failures trigger catastrophic agent death (a $-100$ penalty), while the deterministic strategy survives the same episodes.\nOnce death episodes are removed, the performance gap between strategies nearly vanishes.\n\nReaching this conclusion requires a methodological contribution.\nThe standard approach to generating routing labels---per-step oracle comparison---degenerates under sparse rewards.\nIn ScienceWorld, non-zero reward arrives only at episode termination; 97.4\\% of steps (across 11 prescreened task types) produce identical scores regardless of modality, leaving no step-level signal to learn from (\\S\\ref{sec:collection}).\nKeyword-based heuristics also fail structurally, as ScienceWorld actions lack science-specific terminology (\\S\\ref{sec:baselines}).\nWe instead propose \\emph{episode-level counterfactual analysis}: run complete episodes under pure-internal (ReAct \\cite{react-2023}) and pure-deterministic strategies, then compare episode outcomes to generate routing labels (\\S\\ref{sec:collection}).\n\nAcross 11 ScienceWorld task types (245 episode pairs), the full deterministic advantage is $\\Delta_{\\text{full}} = +29.60$ points.\nExcluding death episodes, the gap collapses to $\\Delta_{\\text{nd}} = +2.84$; 75 of 95 non-tie labels (78.9\\%) arise from death asymmetry---a penalty-independent measure.\nThe penalty-sensitive Death Avoidance Factor (DAF; \\S\\ref{sec:daf}) is 90.41\\% at the default penalty $P{=}100$, ranging from 46\\% ($P{=}10$) to 95\\% ($P{=}200$).\nThe per-task correlation between death-rate differential and performance gap is $r = 0.97$ ($p < 10^{-6}$, $n = 11$), confirming that death avoidance is the dominant mechanism across task types (\\S\\ref{sec:death-decomp}).\n\nTwo cross-context checks probe the specificity of this finding.\nFirst, a MATH Level~4--5 evaluation (300 problems), using a code interpreter as the deterministic modality, shows a directional reversal: internal reasoning outperforms code interpreter by $+4.3$ percentage points---the opposite direction from ScienceWorld.\nIn the absence of death environments and introduce episode-level counterfactual analysis with the DAF metric, a methodology for quantifying what fraction of routing signal derives from catastrophic-failure avoidance         "content": "\\section{Method}\n\\label{sec:method}\n\n\\subsection{Problem Setup}\n\\label{sec:problem-setup}\n\nConsider an interactive environment $\\mathcal{E}$ with state space $\\mathcal{S}$, observation space $\\mathcal{O}$, and action space $\\mathcal{A}$. An agent follows a policy $\\pi: \\mathcal{O}^* \\rightarrow \\mathcal{A}$ that maps observation histories to actions. At each step $t$, the agent receives observation $o_t$, selects action $a_t = \\pi(o_1, \\ldots, o_t)$, and the environment transitions to state $s_{t+1}$.\n\nWe define a modality set $\\mathcal{M} = \\{{\\tt int}, {\\tt det}\\}$ governing how the agent processes state transitions:\n\\begin{itemize}\n    \\item \\textbf{Internal} ($m = {\\tt int}$): The agent uses its own generation to predict intermediate observations. The LLM interleaves chain-of-thought reasoning with environment actions following the ReAct paradigm \\cite{react-2023}, but prediction errors compound across steps.\n    \\item \\textbf{Deterministic} ($m = {\\tt det}$): The agent receives ground-truth observations from the environment simulator at each step---equivalent to access to a perfect dynamics model. Action selection remains with the LLM; only the state-transition prediction is replaced.\n\\end{itemize}\n\nA \\emph{routing policy} $\\rho: \\mathcal{O}^* \\rightarrow \\mathcal{M}$ selects which modality to use at each step. The goal of modality routing is to learn $\\rho$ that maximizes expected episode return. Our analysis investigates what signal is available to learn such a router.\n\n\\subsection{Counterfactual Episode Collection}\n\\label{sec:collection}\n\nPer-step oracle labeling assigns routing labels by comparing single-step outcomes under each computation modality. Under sparse terminal rewards, this approach degenerates: on ScienceWorld \\cite{scienceworld-2022}, 97.4\\% of steps (across 11 prescreened task types) produce identical intermediate scores regardless of modality, yielding no routing signal. We instead perform episode-level counterfactual analysis.\n\n\\paragraph{Pure-strategy trajectories.}\nFor a task instance $t$ and modality $m \\in \\mathcal{M}$, a \\emph{pure-strategy trajectory} is the complete episode obtained by applying modality $m$ at every step:\n\\begin{equation}\n    \\tau_m^{(t)} = (o_1, a_1, o_2, a_2, \\ldots, o_T, a_T)\n\\end{equation}\nwhere $T \\leq T_{\\max}$ is the episode length (capped at $T_{\\max} = 30$ steps). Both trajectories $\\tau_{\\tt int}^{(t)}$ and $\\tau_{\\tt det}^{(t)}$ are executed under identical initial conditions (same random seed, same task variation), ensuring that performance differences arise solely from the modality.\n\nEach trajectory $\\tau$ yields a terminal score $s(\\tau) \\in \\mathbb{Z}$ and a death indicator $d(\\tau) \\in \\{0, 1\\}$. When the agent dies ($d = 1$), the environment imposes a penalty: $s(\\tau) = -P$ where $P > 0$ ($P = 100$ in ScienceWorld). The episode pair produces a tuple:\n\\begin{multline}\n    \\bigl(s^{\\tt int}, s^{\\tt det}, d^{\\tt int}, d^{\\tt det}\\bigr) \\triangleq \\\\\n    \\bigl(s(\\tau_{\\tt int}),\\, s(\\tau_{\\tt det}),\\, d(\\tau_{\\tt int}),\\, d(\\tau_{\\tt det})\\bigr)\n\\end{multline}\n\nWe use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (vLLM) on ScienceWorld \\cite{scienceworld-2022}, a text-based environment spanning 30 task types with a $-100$ death penalty. After prescreening, we collect 245 episode pairs across 11 task types (20--40 per type).\n\n\\subsection{Episode-Level Labeling}\n\\label{sec:labeling}\n\nWe define a labeling function $L$ that maps a counterfactual pair to a routing preference:\n\\begin{multline}\n    L\\!\\bigl(\\tau_{\\tt int}^{(t)}, \\tau_{\\tt det}^{(t)}\\bigr) \\;\\rightarrow \\\\\n    \\ell \\in \\{{\\tt det\\text{-}pref},\\; {\\tt int\\text{-}pref},\\; {\\tt no\\text{-}pref}\\}\n\\end{multline}\n\nThe labeling function is \\emph{death-aware}: it prioritizes survival over score, reflecting the asymmetric cost of catastrophic failure in interactive environments. ScienceWorld scores are integer-valued, so we use exact (in)equality with no threshold. The full procedure is given in Algorithm~\\ref{alg:labeling}. Figure~\\ref{fig:pipeline} illustrates the overall pipeline.\n\n\\begin{figure}[t]\n\\centering\n\\includegraphics[width=\\columnwidth]{figures/pipeline_overview.pdf}\n\\caption{Counterfactual episode collection and analysis pipeline. Each task instance is run under both pure strategies independently, producing episode-level labels via Algorithm~\\ref{alg:labeling}.}\n\\label{fig:pipeline}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\begin{algorithm}[t]\n\\caption{Episode-Level Counterfactual Labeling}\n\\label{alg:labeling}\n\\begin{algorithmic}[1]\n\\REQUIRE Task instance $t$, modalities $\\mathcal{M} = \\{{\\tt int}, {\\tt det}\\}$\n\\ENSURE Label $\\ell \\in \\{{\\tt det\\text{-}pref}, {\\tt int\\text{-}pref}, {\\tt no\\text{-}pref}\\}$\n\\FOR{each $m \\in \\mathcal{M}$}\n    \\STATE Run episode $\\tau_m$ with pure-strategy $m$\n    \\STATE Record score $s_m$ and death indicator $d_m$\n\\ENDFOR\n\\IF{$d_{\\tt int} = 1$ \\AND $d_{\\tt det} = 0$}\n    \\STATE $\\ell \\leftarrow {\\tt det\\text{-}pref}$ \\COMMENT{death asymmetry}\n\\ELSIF{$d_{\\tt int} = 0$ \\AND $d_{\\tt det} = 1$}\n    \\STATE $\\ell \\leftarrow {\\tt int\\text{-}pref}$ \\COMMENT{death asymmetry}\n\\ELSIF{$d_{\\tt int} = d_{\\tt det} = 1$}\n    \\STATE $\\ell \\leftarrow {\\tt no\\text{-}pref}$ \\COMMENT{both dead}\n\\ELSIF{$s_{\\tt det} > s_{\\tt int}$}\n    \\STATE $\\ell \\leftarrow {\\tt det\\text{-}pref}$ \\COMMENT{score comparison}\n\\ELSIF{$s_{\\tt int} > s_{\\tt det}$}\n    \\STATE $\\ell \\leftarrow {\\tt int\\text{-}pref}$ \\COMMENT{score comparison}\n\\ELSE\n    \\STATE $\\ell \\leftarrow {\\tt no\\text{-}pref}$ \\COMMENT{tied alive}\n\\ENDIF\n\\RETURN $\\ell$\n\\end{algorithmic}\n\\end{algorithm}\n\nThe four mutually exclusive cases correspond to:\n\\begin{enumerate}\n    \\item \\textbf{Death asymmetry} (lines 5--8): $d^{\\tt int} \\neq d^{\\tt det}$ $\\rightarrow$ the surviving strategy is preferred. This accounts for 78.9\\% of all non-tie labels.\n    \\item \\textbf{Both dead} (lines 9--10): $d^{\\tt int} = d^{\\tt det} = 1$ $\\rightarrow$ ${\\tt no\\_preference}$.\n    \\item \\textbf{Score comparison} (lines 11--14): both survive and $s^{\\tt det} \\neq s^{\\tt int}$ $\\rightarrow$ the higher-scoring strategy is preferred.\n    \\item \\textbf{Tied alive} (lines 15--16): both survive and $s^{\\tt det} = s^{\\tt int}$ $\\rightarrow$ ${\\tt no\\_preference}$.\n\\end{enumerate}\n\nLabel distributions are reported in \\S\\ref{sec:death-decomp}.\n\n\\subsection{Death Avoidance Factor}\n\\label{sec:daf}\n\nTo quantify the contribution of death avoidance to routing signal, we decompose the mean score gap between strategies. Let $\\delta = \\mathbb{E}[d^{\\tt int}] - \\mathbb{E}[d^{\\tt det}]$ denote the death-rate differential and $\\Delta_{\\text{nd}}$ the mean score gap restricted to episodes where neither strategy dies. The full gap decomposes as:\n\\begin{equation}\n    \\Delta_{\\text{full}} \\approx \\underbrace{\\delta \\cdot P}_{\\text{death contribution}} + \\Delta_{\\text{nd}}\n\\end{equation}\nThe approximation holds exactly when the surviving strategy scores zero in all death-asymmetry episodes; in our data, the residual is small ($29.60 - 29.37 = 0.23$, or $0.8\\%$ of $\\Delta_{\\text{full}}$).\n\nWe define the Death Avoidance Factor (DAF) as the fraction of the full score gap attributable to death avoidance:\n\\begin{equation}\n    \\text{DAF} = 1 - \\frac{\\Delta_{\\text{nd}}}{\\Delta_{\\text{full}}} \\approx \\frac{\\delta P}{\\delta P + \\Delta_{\\text{nd}}}\n\\end{equation}%\n\\footnote{When $\\Delta_{\\text{nd}} < 0$ (deterministic strategy scores lower than internal on non-death episodes), DAF exceeds 1, indicating death avoidance overcompensates for a non-death disadvantage.}\n\nDAF is well-defined when $\\Delta_{\\text{full}} > 0$; in our data, the minimum per-task $\\Delta_{\\text{full}}$ is $+9.58$ (\\texttt{find-non-living-thing}), ensuring numerical stability. Since DAF $= \\delta P / (\\delta P + \\Delta_{\\text{nd}})$, it increases monotonically with $P$---a mathematical consequence, not an empirical finding. We therefore report both DAF at the environment default ($P{=}100$) and the penalty-independent death-asymmetry label fraction (78.9\\%).\n\nTo assess sensitivity to penalty magnitude, we recalculate DAF under hypothetical death penalties (Appendix~\\ref{app:penalty}): $P{=}10 \\rightarrow$ DAF $= 46.4\\%$, $P{=}50 \\rightarrow 81.2\\%$, $P{=}100 \\rightarrow 89.6\\%$, $P{=}200 \\rightarrow 94.5\\%$. Death avoidance remains the dominant component across all penalty magnitudes, though its relative contribution scales with penalty severity. As a penalty-independent companion metric, 75 of 95 non-tie routing labels (78.9\\%) are driven by death asymmetry rather than score comparison (\\S\\ref{sec:labeling}), confirming that death avoidance dominates routing signal regardless of penalty magnitude.\n",

        "content": "\\documentclass[11pt]{article}\n\n\\usepackage[review]{acl}\n\n\\usepackage{times}\n\\usepackage{latexsym}\n\\usepackage[T1]{fontenc}\n\\usepackage[utf8]{inputenc}\n\\usepackage{microtype}\n\\usepackage{graphicx}\n\\graphicspath{{figures/}}\n\\usepackage{booktabs}\n\\usepackage{amsmath}\n\\usepackage{amssymb}\n\\usepackage{algorithm}\n\\usepackage{algorithmic}\n\n\\title{Death Avoidance as the Dominant Routing Signal:\\\\A Counterfactual Analysis on ScienceWorld}\n\n\\author{Anonymous}\n\n\\begin{document}\n\\maketitle\n\n\\input{abstract}\n\\input{introduction}\n\\input{method}\n\\input{experiments}\n\\input{related_work}\n\\input{discussion}\n\\input{conclusion}\n\n\\section*{Limitations}\n\nOur analysis uses a single benchmark (ScienceWorld) with a single LLM backbone (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct), and generalization to other interactive environments and model scales remains to be established. A preliminary cross-model pilot with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ($N{=}10$ episode pairs, 2 task types) shows directionally consistent death patterns (\\S\\ref{sec:cross-model}), but full-scale multi-model validation remains future work. The $-100$ death penalty may amplify DAF; environments with less catastrophic penalties could exhibit lower DAF, though the qualitative finding may still hold. On the 135 episodes (55.1\\%) where neither strategy leads to catastrophic failure, deterministic computation retains a small advantage ($\\Delta_{\\text{nd}} = +2.84$), indicating non-zero routing signal beyond death avoidance. Our analysis covers 11 of 30 ScienceWorld task types; the remaining 19 (63\\%) were excluded during prescreening because both strategies timed out on all seed variations within the 30-step budget, providing no counterfactual signal. These tasks likely require longer-horizon planning; increasing the step budget could surface additional routing signal whose composition may differ from the death-dominated pattern observed here. Stronger models (e.g., 70B-scale or reasoning-specialized) likely exhibit lower internal-strategy death rates, which would reduce DAF. Our finding may reflect a capability-dependent failure mode: at higher capability levels, death avoidance may no longer dominate routing signal.\n\n\\paragraph{Cross-environment scope.}\nOur MATH and ALFWorld analyses (\\S\\ref{sec:discussion}) provide cross-environment evidence but do not conclusively establish generalization. In MATH (no death penalty), the deterministic advantage vanishes with a directional reversal favoring internal reasoning ($+4.3$\\,pp, not statistically significant). In ALFWorld, the deterministic advantage stems from a capability gap rather than death avoidance. Environments with graded failure costs or intermediate penalty regimes remain unstudied.\n\n\\paragraph{Step-level mislabeling.} Episode-level labels may assign suboptimal routing decisions to individual steps; in particular, steps preceding a death event are labeled det-preferred even if the death was not foreseeable from those steps' observations. Training on pure-strategy trajectories but deploying on mixed policy also introduces a distribution shift \\citep{dagger-2011}.\n\n\\paragraph{Scope.}\nExtending the counterfactual methodology to environments with graded failure costs, embodied agents, or multi-turn dialogue systems would clarify how broadly death avoidance accounts for apparent routing signal. Step-level labeling with denser rewards and the logit--generation gap in the implicit router are natural next steps. We audit labeling quality in Appendix~\\ref{app:labeling}.\n\n\\section*{Ethics Statement}\n\nThis work uses ScienceWorld \\cite{scienceworld-2022}, a publicly available text-based simulation environment, and does not involve human subjects or private data. All language models are accessed via standard APIs or publicly released weights. We report computational costs: approximately 40 GPU-hours on two RTX 5090 GPUs for data collection, router training, and evaluation.\n\n\\bibliography{references}\n\n\\appendix\n\n\\section{Labeling Quality Audit}\n\\label{app:labeling}\n\nA potential concern is oracle circularity: whether episode-level labels reflect tie-breaking artifacts rather than genuine modality differences. We audit all 245 labels. Of the 150 \\texttt{no\\_preference} labels (61.2\\%), 115 (46.9\\%) are both-alive ties and 35 (14.3\\%) are both-dead---all excluded from router training. The remaining 95 training labels are entirely genuine: 75 from death asymmetry (70 deterministic-preferred, 5 internal-preferred) and 20 from score comparison with both strategies surviving (16 deterministic-preferred, 4 internal-preferred). Zero labels depend on tie-breaking. Retraining the router using only death-asymmetry labels yields balanced accuracy of 57.3\\%, within 1$\\sigma$ of the full-label retrain (57.6 $\\pm$ 0.5\\%), confirming that score-comparison labels contribute negligible additional signal. The 97.4\\% step-level tie rate (\\S\\ref{sec:collection}) further motivates episode-level over step-level labeling.\n\n\\section{Per-Task Decomposition}\n\\label{app:per-task}\nWe select 11 of ScienceWorld's 30 task types via prescreening: task types where both strategies complete at least one episode within the 30-step budget are retained; types where both strategies time out on all seed variations are excluded.\\footnote{Prescreening ensures that the counterfactual comparison is meaningful---task types where neither strategy makes progress provide no routing signal.}\n\n\\begin{table}[h]\n\\centering\n\\scriptsize\n\\setlength{\\tabcolsep}{2.5pt}\n\\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrccc@{}}\n\\toprule\nTask & $n$ & $\\Delta_\\text{full}$ & D\\%\\textsubscript{int} & D\\%\\textsubscript{det} & D / I / N \\\\\n\\midrule\nid-life-stages-1       & 20  & $+47.50$ & 55   & 10   & 9 / 0 / 11  \\\\\nlifespan-long          & 25  & $+44.00$ & 56   & 16   & 11 / 1 / 13 \\\\\nlifespan-l-then-s      & 20  & $+40.80$ & 45   & 10   & 8 / 1 / 11  \\\\\ninclined-plane         & 20  & $+36.00$ & 55   & 20   & 7 / 0 / 13  \\\\\nfreeze                 & 20  & $+30.50$ & 55   & 25   & 6 / 0 / 14  \\\\\nmeas-melt-point        & 20  & $+30.05$ & 55   & 25   & 6 / 0 / 14  \\\\\nid-life-stages-2       & 20  & $+30.00$ & 50   & 20   & 6 / 0 / 14  \\\\\nfind-animal            & 20  & $+26.65$ & 50   & 25   & 5 / 0 / 15  \\\\\ngrow-fruit             & 20  & $+25.10$ & 45   & 20   & 6 / 1 / 13  \\\\\nchem-mix               & 20  & $+21.80$ & 45   & 25   & 6 / 2 / 12  \\\\\n\\midrule\nfind-non-living$^\\dagger$ & 40 & $+9.58$ & 0  & 0    & 16 / 4 / 20 \\\\\n\\midrule\n\\textbf{All (11 tasks)} & \\textbf{245} & $\\mathbf{+29.60}$ & \\textbf{42.9} & \\textbf{16.3} & \\textbf{86 / 9 / 150} \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\caption{Per-task decomposition of the death avoidance effect. D\\%: death rate for internal (int) and deterministic (det) strategies. D/I/N: episode labels (det-preferred / internal-preferred / no-preference). Sorted by $\\Delta_{\\text{full}}$ descending. $\\dagger$\\,Only task with zero deaths under both strategies.}\n\\label{tab:per-task}\n\\end{table}\n\n\\section{Correlation Robustness}\n\\label{app:correlation}\n\nThe Pearson $r = 0.9698$ reported in \\S\\ref{sec:death-decomp} is robust across multiple diagnostics. Spearman rank correlation is $\\rho = 0.986$ ($p = 2.4 \\times 10^{-8}$), confirming that the relationship is not driven by outliers or non-linearity. A nonparametric bootstrap (10{,}000 resamples) yields 95\\% CI $[0.952, 0.995]$.\n\n\\begin{table}[h]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\begin{tabular}{@{}lr@{}}\n\\toprule\nTask removed & $r_{\\text{LOO}}$ \\\\\n\\midrule\nid-life-stages-1       & 0.963 \\\\\nlifespan-long          & 0.969 \\\\\nlifespan-l-then-s      & 0.976 \\\\\ninclined-plane         & 0.969 \\\\\nfreeze                 & 0.971 \\\\\nmeas-melt-point        & 0.972 \\\\\nid-life-stages-2       & 0.972 \\\\\nfind-animal            & 0.970 \\\\\ngrow-fruit             & 0.973 \\\\\nchem-mix               & 0.969 \\\\\nfind-non-living        & 0.980 \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\caption{Leave-one-out Pearson $r$ for the death rate differential vs.\\ $\\Delta_{\\text{full}}$ correlation. Full $r = 0.970$; LOO range $[0.963, 0.980]$. No single task type is a leverage point.}\n\\label{tab:loo}\n\\end{table}\n\n\\section{Router Training Details}\n\\label{app:router-details}\n\nWe use Qwen3-1.7B for the router to avoid circular dependency with the Qwen2.5-7B data-generating model.\n\nGradient accumulation is critical for the implicit router: with gradient accumulation of 1, the model fails to achieve meaningful routing discrimination (internal recall 26.7\\%); with gradient accumulation of 8, the model becomes non-degenerate (internal recall above 50\\% across all seeds). All main-text results use gradient accumulation 8.\n\nCross-seed balanced accuracy is stable (57--59\\%), but internal recall varies from 51.5\\% to 81.8\\%, reflecting the structurally thin learnable signal: when ${\\sim}90\\%$ of routing value is death avoidance, the non-death signal is inherently noisy. Deployed end-to-end, the trained router allocates 97.0\\% of episodes to deterministic computation with 17.6\\% death rate, and misrouting cost (death from internally-routed episodes) exceeds the benefit of correctly routing rare internal-preferred cases.\n\n\\begin{table}[h]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\resizebox{\\columnwidth}{!}{%\n\\begin{tabular}{@{}lcc@{}}\n\\toprule\nHyperparameter & Classification Head & Implicit Router \\\\\n\\midrule\nBase model & Qwen3-1.7B & Qwen3-1.7B \\\\\nArchitecture & Linear + LoRA & SFT + LoRA \\\\\nLoRA $r$ / $\\alpha$ & 16 / 32 & 16 / 32 \\\\\nLearning rate & 2e-5 & 2e-4 \\\\\nOptimizer & AdamW & AdamW \\\\\nEpochs & 3 & 3 \\\\\nBatch size (per device) & 4 & 4 \\\\\nGradient accumulation & 8 & 8 \\\\\nWarmup ratio & 0.1 & 0.1 \\\\\nWeight decay & 0.01 & 0.01 \\\\\nMax sequence length & 512 & 512 \\\\\nSeeds & \\{42\\} & \\{42, 123, 456, 789\\} \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}}\n\\caption{Router training hyperparameters. Both architectures use the same base model with LoRA adaptation. The classification head degenerates across all configurations; the implicit router results are reported as 4-seed mean$\\pm$std.}\n\\label{tab:hyperparams}\n\\end{table}\n\n\\section{Penalty Sensitivity Analysis}\n\\label{app:penalty}\n\n\\begin{table}[h]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\begin{tabular}{@{}rrrr@{}}\n\\toprule\n$P$ & $\\Delta_{\\text{full}}(P)$ & $\\Delta_{\\text{nd}}$ & DAF($P$) \\\\\n\\midrule\n10 & 5.72 & 3.07 & 46.4\\% \\\\\n25 & 9.70 & 3.07 & 68.4\\% \\\\\n50 & 16.33 & 3.07 & 81.2\\% \\\\\n100 & 29.60 & 3.07 & 89.6\\%\\textsuperscript{*} \\\\\n200 & 56.13 & 3.07 & 94.5\\% \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}\n\\caption{Sensitivity of $\\Delta_{\\text{full}}$ and DAF to death penalty magnitude $P$. $\\Delta_{\\text{full}}(P) \\approx \\delta \\cdot P + \\Delta_{\\text{nd}}$, where $\\delta = 0.2653$ is the death-rate differential. $\\Delta_{\\text{nd}} = 3.07$ here includes both-died episodes in the non-death pool, yielding DAF=89.6\\% at $P{=}100$ versus 90.41\\% in the main text (\\S\\ref{sec:death-decomp}), which uses strict neither-died filtering ($\\Delta_{\\text{nd}} = 2.84$). \\textsuperscript{*}Default setting.}\n\\label{tab:penalty-sensitivity}\n\\end{table}\n\n\\end{document}\n",

        "content": "\\section{Experiments}\n\n\\subsection{Death Avoidance Decomposition}\n\\label{sec:death-decomp}\n\n\\begin{figure}[t]\n\\centering\n\\includegraphics[width=\\columnwidth]{figures/fig1_daf_scatter.pdf}\n\\caption{Per-task scatter plot: death rate differential (internal minus deterministic) vs.\\ performance gap ($\\Delta_{\\text{full}}$). Pearson $r = 0.9698$ ($p = 8.12 \\times 10^{-7}$). Each point is one of 11 ScienceWorld task types.}\n\\label{fig:decomposition}\n\\end{figure}\n\nThe full performance gap between deterministic and internal strategies across 245 episodes is $\\Delta_{\\text{full}} = +29.60$ points. When we exclude all episodes where either strategy results in agent death, the gap collapses to $\\Delta_{\\text{nd}} = +2.84$. The resulting Death Avoidance Factor (\\S\\ref{sec:daf}) is 90.41\\%: approximately 90\\% of the deterministic strategy's advantage over internal reasoning is attributable to death avoidance rather than superior task performance when both agents survive.\n\nThis concentration is consistent across task types (Appendix~\\ref{app:per-task}). The Pearson correlation between per-task death rate differential and $\\Delta_{\\text{full}}$ is $r = 0.9698$ ($p = 8.12 \\times 10^{-7}$; bootstrap 95\\% CI $[0.952, 0.995]$), as shown in Figure~\\ref{fig:decomposition}. Spearman rank correlation is $\\rho = 0.986$ ($p = 2.4 \\times 10^{-8}$), and leave-one-out analysis shows $r \\in [0.963, 0.980]$---no single task type is a leverage point (Appendix~\\ref{app:correlation}). We note that death rate differential and $\\Delta_{\\text{full}}$ are structurally coupled through the penalty term $P$, so high correlation is expected when death dominates. The empirically non-trivial finding is that 78.9\\% of non-tie routing labels are driven by death asymmetry independent of $P$. Knowing how much more frequently the internal strategy dies is nearly sufficient to predict the full performance gap for a given task type. The internal strategy dies in 42.9\\% of episodes compared to 16.3\\% for deterministic computation---a 2.6$\\times$ ratio that drives the bulk of the observed score difference.\n\nThe episode-level label distribution reflects this asymmetry: of 245 episodes, 86 are \\texttt{det\\_preferred}, only 9 \\texttt{internal\\_preferred}, and 150 \\texttt{no\\_preference}---when internal reasoning does not cause death, it performs comparably to deterministic computation.\n\nNotably, the per-task DAF distribution is bimodal: \\texttt{find-non-living-thing} exhibits DAF $\\approx 0\\%$ (routing signal entirely from non-death score differences, $\\Delta = +9.58$), while all other task types exceed 85\\%.\n\nOne task reveals the residual non-death signal. \\texttt{find-non-living-thing} ($n=40$) has zero deaths under both strategies yet shows $\\Delta_{\\text{full}} = +9.58$, entirely from non-death performance differences---deterministic computation can provide advantages through more accurate state tracking even when agents survive. However, among the 10 death-prone task types, death avoidance overwhelms non-death differences. When both modalities survive, the gap is small but non-negligible ($\\Delta_{\\text{nd}} = +2.84$, 9.6\\% of $\\Delta_{\\text{full}}$).\n\n\\subsection{Baselines}\n\\label{sec:baselines}\n\n\\begin{table}[t]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\resizebox{\\columnwidth}{!}{%\n\\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}\n\\toprule\nStrategy & Score & 95\\% CI & Death \\% \\\\\n\\midrule\nAlways-Internal & $-39.07$ & [$-46.40$, $-32.27$] & 42.9 \\\\\nAlways-Deterministic & $-9.47$ & [$-14.71$, $-4.29$] & 16.3 \\\\\nRandom & $-22.38$ & [$-28.67$, $-15.75$] & 27.8 \\\\\nOracle & $-6.58$ & [$-11.54$, $-1.70$] & 14.3 \\\\\n\\midrule\nTrained Router$^\\dagger$ & $-10.70$ & [$-16.33$, $-5.27$] & 17.6 \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}}\n\\caption{Episode-weighted mean scores on ScienceWorld (11 task types, 245 episodes). 95\\% Bootstrap CIs. The oracle selects the higher-scoring strategy per episode; 96.3\\% of its decisions match the always-deterministic strategy. $\\dagger$\\,4-seed mean.}\n\\label{tab:baselines}\n\\end{table}\n\nTable~\\ref{tab:baselines} reports episode-weighted mean scores and death rates for four unconditional strategies. Always-deterministic ($-9.47$) outperforms always-internal ($-39.07$) by 29.60 points, consistent with $\\Delta_{\\text{full}}$. The oracle, which selects the higher-scoring strategy per episode, improves only modestly to $-6.58$, with 96.3\\% of its routing decisions matching always-deterministic. This \\emph{oracle degeneracy} indicates that the optimal episode-level routing policy closely resembles unconditional deterministic computation---the routing signal is insufficient to improve upon simply always choosing the deterministic strategy. Random routing ($-22.38$) falls between the two pure strategies, with a death rate (27.8\\%) proportional to its 50/50 allocation.\n\nKeyword-based routing fails structurally: match rates cluster at extremes (85.8\\% or $<$5\\%), precluding meaningful routing discrimination.\n\n\\subsection{Router Training as Diagnostic}\n\\label{sec:router-diagnostic}\n\nA natural question is whether the episode-level counterfactual labels can train a step-level router. We investigate this as a diagnostic probe of label informativeness rather than a routing system proposal, testing two architectures.\n\n\\paragraph{Classification head.} A linear head on LLM hidden representations, trained on episode-level labels, degenerates to always-deterministic (0\\% internal recall) across all configurations (class weighting, focal loss, undersampling, temperature scaling).\n\n\\paragraph{Implicit router.} We fine-tune Qwen3-1.7B to internalize routing decisions within its generation (Appendix~\\ref{app:router-details}). Across four seeds, balanced accuracy is $58.1 \\pm 0.8\\%$---above chance but insufficient for practical routing, with seed-level variation (Appendix~\\ref{app:router-details}) reflecting threshold sensitivity rather than genuine signal.\n\n\\paragraph{End-to-end evaluation.} Deployed as an episode-level router (Table~\\ref{tab:baselines}), the trained router scores $-10.70$ (95\\% CI $[-16.33, -5.27]$), not statistically outperforming always-deterministic ($-9.47$, $[-14.71, -4.29]$; overlapping CIs). The episode-to-step granularity mismatch is the bottleneck: when DAF $\\approx 90\\%$, router headroom is limited to the ${\\sim}10\\%$ non-death signal.\n\n\\paragraph{Data split.} Of 245 episodes, 95 non-tie labels are split 85/15 (81 train, 14 validation; 1734/306 steps). Baselines in Table~\\ref{tab:baselines} report trajectory statistics; the router score ($-10.70$) comes from fresh environment interaction.\n\n\\paragraph{Labeling quality.} We verify label quality in Appendix~\\ref{app:labeling}.\n\n\\subsection{Cross-Model Verification}\n\\label{sec:cross-model}\n\nTo test whether the death avoidance pattern is model-specific, we run a mechanism verification pilot with Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on two task types (\\texttt{freeze} and \\texttt{find-non-living-thing}, 5 episode pairs each, $N{=}10$). Llama-8B achieves lower absolute ScienceWorld scores than Qwen-2.5-7B, reflecting weaker task-level capability, but the death pattern direction is consistent across model families.\n\nOn \\texttt{freeze}, the internal strategy dies in 40\\% of episodes versus 20\\% for deterministic (Qwen: 55\\%/25\\%)---the same directional asymmetry. The single non-tie episode arises from death asymmetry: the internal strategy dies while deterministic survives, producing a det-preferred label consistent with the Qwen pattern. On \\texttt{find-non-living-thing}, both strategies achieve 0\\% death rate under Llama, matching Qwen exactly; the 3 det-preferred labels arise from non-death score differences.\n\n\\begin{table}[t]\n\\centering\n\\small\n\\resizebox{\\columnwidth}{!}{%\n\\begin{tabular}{@{}llcccc@{}}\n\\toprule\nTask & Model & D\\%\\textsubscript{int} & D\\%\\textsubscript{det} & $\\Delta$D\\% & D / I / N \\\\\n\\midrule\nfreeze & Qwen-7B & 55 & 25 & +30 & 6 / 0 / 14 \\\\\nfreeze & Llama-8B & 40 & 20 & +20 & 1 / 0 / 4 \\\\\n\\midrule\nfind-non-living & Qwen-7B & 0 & 0 & 0 & 16 / 4 / 20 \\\\\nfind-non-living & Llama-8B & 0 & 0 & 0 & 3 / 1 / 1 \\\\\n\\bottomrule\n\\end{tabular}}\n\\caption{Cross-model death rate comparison. Llama pilot: $n{=}5$ episodes per task; Qwen: from Table~\\ref{tab:per-task}. $\\Delta$D\\%: internal minus deterministic death rate. D/I/N: det-preferred / internal-preferred / no-preference labels.}\n\\label{tab:cross-model}\n\\end{table}\n\nTable~\\ref{tab:cross-model} summarizes the comparison. This pilot ($N{=}10$ episode pairs) provides preliminary directional evidence only: the sample size precludes statistical claims. Nevertheless, observing the same death asymmetry direction in a different model family (Llama vs.\\ Qwen) suggests that the pattern reflects a structural property of internal reasoning in interactive environments rather than a model-specific artifact.",
